title: A Dark Bedroom May Be Better for Your Heart
paragraphs: Your bedroom may look dark when you turn off the lights, but is it really?
Light can still creep in through the curtains or under the door, or shine out from the small lights on electronic devices. And new research suggests that even low light at night may affect the heart.

The study, published in the European Heart Journal, included more than 11,000 adults in the UK. The participants wore devices that measured their nighttime light exposure for seven days. Three years later, the researchers used heart scans to look at the structure and function of their hearts.

People exposed to more than three lux of light at night were more likely to have thicker walls in the heart's left ventricle — one of its main chambers. Their heart muscles also showed signs of being less able to flex normally during a heartbeat, which can signal early heart problems.

And three lux isn't very bright — it's equivalent to light coming under a closed bedroom door. But previous research has shown that even this low level of light can affect melatonin, a hormone that helps control sleep.
That may be one reason nighttime light affects the heart. It can shorten sleep and disturb the body's natural 24-hour clock, both of which can impact blood pressure and heart function.

However, the study does not prove that light directly caused the heart changes. The researchers also measured light exposure for only one week, which may not fully represent people's long-term habits.

Still, experts say reducing light at night could be a simple way to protect your heart health. They suggest using blackout curtains, choosing warmer bedside lighting and covering lights on electronic devices.
Experts also recommend dimming the lights in the hours before bedtime, since evening light can disrupt the body's natural sleep-wake cycle even before you fall asleep.
So tonight, it might be worth checking just how dark your bedroom really is.
